If any fisher’s total exceeds 2.5kg, the excess must be returned to the lake or deposited into a community reserve. If the weekly total exceeds 20% of the lake’s mass, the excess is returned. If a fisher fails to correct an excess within 48 hours, they lose fishing permission for one week. Random checks by community members and a weekly meeting to update lake mass and recalculate the 20% cap ensure compliance.
agent_2.reasoning: This rule balances short‑term needs with long‑term sustainability by limiting individual impact and keeping total harvest in line with the lake’s natural replenishment rate. The 2.5kg cap keeps each trip modest, reducing overfishing risk, while the dynamic 20% weekly cap adapts to the lake’s size and keeps total catch proportional to available biomass. The ledger and community oversight foster transparency and collective responsibility, protecting our future harvests and ensuring that everyone’s livelihood can persist.

agent_3.policy: Each fisher may take at most 4% of the lake's current stock per trip, and all fish must be reported to the community ledger; the community maintains a 15% reserve of the lake's stock for safety.
agent_3.operationalization: On each fishing day, each fisher records the weight of fish caught on a shared ledger. The community calculates the lake’s current stock, applies the 4% cap, and if the total catch would exceed the 15% reserve, the surplus is returned to the community pool and redistributed to those with lower reserves. Non‑compliance results in a penalty equal to the excess weight, which must be returned in the next trip or paid as a community contribution. Monthly meetings adjust the cap if the lake stock falls below 80kg.
agent_3.reasoning: This rule protects the fish population by limiting individual take and keeping a safety reserve, while also ensuring that all community members have fair access and a reliable food source. The reporting and penalty system keeps the rule enforceable without heavy bureaucracy, and the reserve keeps the lake healthy for future generations.

agent_4.policy: Each fisher may take no more than 3 % of the lake’s current biomass on any single day, and 10 % of that catch must be deposited into a communal reserve that is used to support restocking and maintenance of the lake.
agent_4.operationalization: Every day a fisher records their catch in the community ledger, noting biomass and reserve deposit. The ledger is reviewed weekly by a rotating committee of three fishers. If a fisher exceeds the 3 % limit or fails to deposit the 10 % reserve, their fishing privileges are suspended for the remainder of the month and they must repay the reserve from future catches. The communal reserve is used annually to fund re‑stocking, habitat improvement and to support fishers in emergency months.
agent_4.reasoning: I propose this so we keep the lake healthy for the long term. A 3 % cap prevents over‑harvesting on any single day, while the 10 % reserve ensures we always have fish left to reproduce and we can replenish stock when needed. Recording catches keeps everyone honest and allows us to see how the lake changes over time. Penalties keep the rule respected, and the reserve gives us a safety net for tough seasons.

agent_5.policy: Each fisherman may keep up to 12 kg of fish per trip; any excess must be released back into the lake.
agent_5.operationalization: After each trip, every fisher records their catch in a communal ledger. They may keep up to 12 kg; if they exceed that, the excess is released immediately and the fisher pays a fine of 0.5 kg of fish per excess kg. The ledger is reviewed at the weekly community gathering, and anyone who fails to comply has their entire catch confiscated until they pay the fine. A rotating group of volunteers enforces the record‑keeping and fines, and the fines are used to fund fish‑stock monitoring and restoration.
agent_5.reasoning: I want a generous personal quota that keeps me profitable while still giving the community a clear, enforceable limit. The ledger and fine system keeps people honest, protects the lake from overfishing, and gives me a predictable share of the catch.

agent_6.policy: Each fisher may take up to 12% of the lake’s current weight per trip, and must deposit 10% of their catch into a communal reserve that is used only for lake replenishment and to support fishers whose reserves fall below 5 kg.
agent_6.operationalization: Before each trip, the fisher computes 12% of the lake’s current weight and caps their catch at that amount. They set aside 10% of the actual catch into a communal ledger; any excess beyond the 12% cap must be allocated entirely to the reserve. The reserve is replenished only when the lake’s weight falls below 100 kg. Compliance is verified by the community chair after each round; a fisher who fails to deposit the required 10% will have their next quota reduced to 6% of lake weight until they catch up.
agent_6.reasoning: I want to keep a big share of the lake for myself, but I also need to ensure the lake stays healthy for future trips. The 12% cap protects the lake from over‑harvest, while the 10% reserve gives a safety net for me and others if my own reserves dip. The rule is simple enough that the community can enforce it and it balances short‑term gain with long‑term sustainability.

agent_7.policy: Each fisher may take at most 10kg per trip, must take at least 1kg; if the lake level falls below 100kg, the maximum drops to 5kg.
agent_7.operationalization: At the communal landing each fisher writes their catch on the shared ledger before leaving. A rotating community monitor reviews the ledger every week and checks the latest lake stock assessment. If a fisher exceeds the limit, they must return the excess to the lake and lose the right to fish for the next round; if they fail to take the minimum 1kg, they receive a warning and a repeat results in a one‑trip ban.
agent_7.reasoning: I need at least 1kg to stay fed and I want to keep the lake healthy so I can keep fishing long term. A 10kg cap keeps the fish population from running out, and the lower 5kg rule when stocks are low protects the lake. The ledger and penalties keep everyone honest and make sure we all survive.

agent_8.policy: Each fisher may take no more than 10% of the lake’s current fish biomass per trip, with a mandatory minimum catch of 1 kg to secure survival.
agent_8.operationalization: At the start of each trip, the community records the current lake biomass on a shared ledger. Each fisher declares their intended catch; the keeper verifies it does not exceed 10% of the recorded biomass. If a fisher exceeds the limit, the surplus is returned to the lake and the fisher’s catch is reduced to 10% (or 1 kg if that is higher). The ledger is updated after every trip, and each fisher’s total monthly catch is capped at 15% of the lake’s average monthly biomass to allow recovery. Non‑compliance results in a one‑trip suspension and a temporary 2 kg reduction in the next month’s minimum quota.
agent_8.reasoning: I need to keep my reserves from dipping below zero, and the lake is already lower than before. A 10% per‑trip cap with a 1 kg survival floor lets me fish aggressively yet sustainably. The monthly 15% cap keeps the whole community from over‑exploiting the lake, giving the fish enough time to rebound. By keeping a public ledger and enforcing penalties, we keep trust and ensure nobody takes more than their fair share, protecting both my livelihood and the lake for future trips.

agent_9.policy: Fishing allowed only when the lake holds at least 150kg; each fisher may net up to 4kg per trip, keeping 1kg for personal sustenance and depositing the remaining 3kg into the community reserve.
agent_9.operationalization: At the start of each trip, a fisher checks the communal lake counter; if it is ≥150kg, they fish up to 4kg. After catching, they record 1kg as personal sustenance and 3kg added to the reserve in a communal ledger. A steward updates the lake level after each cycle. If anyone exceeds 4kg, the excess is returned to the reserve, and if the lake falls below 150kg, all fishing pauses until the reserve restores the lake to 150kg.
agent_9.reasoning: I want to protect the lake so it never runs too low, keep enough food for my family, and give the community a safety net that can refill the lake when it dips. This rule gives clear limits, keeps us all on the same page, and helps us recover from future low‑water periods.

The 25% reserve rule keeps a large bulk of fish in the lake after every trip, protecting the stock for everyone who comes after me.  The ledger and rotating chair give a clear, accountable system.  That balance of personal need and long‑term stewardship is what I need.
